name: อาการปวดหัวหน้าผาก
preview_text: อาการปวดศีรษะตุบๆ ที่หน้าผากหลังรับประทานอาหารมื้อหนัก อาการปวดคล้ายแถบรัดในสภาพอากาศหนาวเย็น และอาการปวดตึงจากการทำงานหนักเกินไป เป็นรูปแบบ TCM ที่แตกต่างกันสามแบบ โดยแต่ละรูปแบบมีสมุนไพรของตัวเอง การ...
categories: ["สภาพหัวหน้า", "อาการปวดหัวและไมเกรน"]
synonyms: ["Anterior Headache", "Forehead Headache", "Frontal Headache", "Headache In The Front Of The Head", "Frontal Head Headache", "Frontal Head Pain", "Pain between the eyebrows or forehead", "Forehead pain", "Sinusitis headache"]
conventional_description: In Western medicine, frontal headaches are most often diagnosed as tension-type headaches, characterized by a band-like pressure or tightness across the forehead. They may also arise from sinus congestion (sinus headaches) or as part of a migraine. Diagnosis is based on symptom description, medical history, and ruling out underlying conditions through physical examination and, when necessary, imaging. The pain is typically managed with over-the-counter analgesics, and chronic cases may involve prescription medications or stress management techniques.
conventional_treatments: Standard treatment relies on over-the-counter pain relievers such as NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen) or acetaminophen. For sinus-related pain, decongestants or antihistamines may be added. Chronic or recurrent frontal headaches are often managed with stress reduction, trigger avoidance, physical therapy, and sometimes preventive medications like tricyclic antidepressants or beta-blockers. Cognitive behavioral therapy can also help patients cope with chronic pain.
tcm_understanding:
In TCM, the forehead is traversed by the Yangming channel, which belongs to the Stomach and Large Intestine. When the Stomach is overheated by rich food, alcohol, or emotional stress, fiery Qi rises along this channel, causing a burning, throbbing pain right between the brows. This is why a frontal headache often follows a heavy meal or a bout of anger-the Stomach simply cannot contain its heat, and it rushes upward.
But not all frontal headaches come from inside. Wind-Cold or Wind-Heat can invade from the outside, especially through the back of the neck, and obstruct the flow of Qi in the head's channels. The pain is often sudden, tight, or distending, and accompanied by cold or flu symptoms. Here, the body's surface is under attack, and the headache is a sign that the defensive Qi is struggling to push the pathogen out.
The Liver is responsible for the smooth flow of Qi. When stress, frustration, or unexpressed anger builds up, Liver Qi stagnates and transforms into heat that surges upward, causing a throbbing, distending pain in the forehead. This pattern is common in people who clench their jaw or feel their headache worsen with anger.
On the other end of the spectrum, a dull, lingering frontal ache that feels worse with fatigue and improves with rest often signals Blood Deficiency-the head simply lacks enough nourishment. And a heavy, foggy pain that feels like a wet towel wrapped around the head points to Phlegm-Dampness from a weak Spleen, where undigested fluids cloud the senses.
classical_quote: 「头痛耳鸣，九窍不利，肠胃之所生也。」
classical_translation: "Headache and tinnitus, when the nine orifices are not functioning smoothly, are generated by the Stomach and Intestines. This early text links frontal headache - as part of general headache - to digestive dysfunction, foreshadowing the Yangming channel’s role."

tcm_diagnosis:
A TCM practitioner begins by asking what the frontal pain actually feels like - is it tight and pressing, throbbing and distending, heavy and foggy, or dull and lingering? Because the forehead sits on the Yangming (Stomach) channel, many frontal headaches involve the Stomach, but the quality of the pain, triggers, and accompanying signs quickly narrow the possibilities.
If the headache arrived suddenly with a cold or flu, the practitioner checks for external invasion. Wind-Cold produces a tight, band-like ache that worsens with cold and draughts, accompanied by chills, no sweating, and a thin white tongue coating. Wind-Heat feels more distending and hot, with fever, thirst, a sore throat, and a tongue that is red with a yellow coat.
When the pain flares with stress, anger, or alcohol, and the person has a red face, bitter taste, and a wiry pulse, Liver Yang Rising is the prime suspect. A heavy, foggy headache that worsens after rich or greasy food, with a greasy tongue coating and a slippery pulse, points to Phlegm-Dampness from a weakened Spleen clouding the head.
A dull, lingering ache that improves with rest, accompanied by a pale face, fatigue, and a thin pulse, suggests Blood Deficiency failing to nourish the head.
If the pain is burning or sharp, worsens with spicy food or heat, and comes with bad breath, swollen gums, or facial heat, the practitioner looks for Stomach Fire - the tongue will be red with a thick yellow coat and the pulse rapid.

patterns.better_with: Cooling foods (cucumber, watermelon), Cold or cool drinks, Rest and lying down, Cold compress on the forehead, Small, light meals
patterns.why_this_happens: The Stomach channel (Yangming) runs directly across the forehead. When rich, spicy food, alcohol, or emotional stress create excess heat in the Stomach, that fire rises along the channel and settles in the forehead, producing a burning, throbbing pain. The pain often flares after a heavy meal because eating fuels the fire and pushes heat upward.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: red body, often with prickles in the centre, thick dry yellow coating. Pulse: rapid (数 shuò), slippery (滑 huá), and forceful, especially strong at the right middle position.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Stomach Fire is an excess heat pattern. Spicy, greasy foods and alcohol directly add more heat to the Stomach, while large meals create stagnation that ferments into fire. Stress and anger stir up Liver Qi, which can invade the Stomach and push heat upward. Cooling foods and drinks directly counteract the heat, while rest helps the body's Qi descend, preventing the upward surge that causes the forehead pain.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Avoid spicy, greasy, fried, and barbecued foods, as well as alcohol and coffee. Eat cooling foods like cucumber, watermelon, celery, and mung beans. Drink plenty of room-temperature or cool water. Eat smaller, lighter meals and try not to eat late at night. A gentle walk after meals helps Stomach Qi descend.

patterns.why_this_happens:
When the Spleen is weak, it cannot properly transform and transport fluids. This leads to an accumulation of dampness, which over time congeals into a thick, turbid substance called phlegm.
Unlike the hot, throbbing pain of Stomach Fire, this phlegm-dampness is heavy and stagnant. It rises along the Stomach channel to the forehead, where it blocks the clear Yang Qi from reaching the head, creating a sensation of heaviness, fogginess, or a dull pressure, often described as a wet cloth wrapped around the head.
Because the root lies in a sluggish digestive system, the headache is usually accompanied by bloating, nausea, a sticky taste, and a heavy, tired feeling in the body.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, swollen, with teeth marks and a thick white greasy coating. Pulse: slippery (滑 huá) and soggy (濡 rú).
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Phlegm-dampness arises when the Spleen’s digestive fire is too weak to process food and fluids. Heavy, greasy, cold, or raw foods further overwhelm the Spleen, creating more dampness that rises to the head. Conversely, warm, cooked meals and gentle movement stoke the digestive fire, helping the Spleen transform and transport fluids. Ginger and cardamom are warming spices that directly dry dampness and settle the stomach, cutting off the supply of turbid phlegm to the head.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Focus on warm, cooked, and easily digestible foods like soups, stews, and congee. Avoid dairy, sugar, greasy fried foods, and excessive raw or cold items, which create more dampness. Gentle daily movement like walking or tai chi helps the Spleen transform fluids. Ginger tea with meals can aid digestion and dispel dampness.

patterns.why_this_happens:
The forehead belongs to the Yangming channel, which relies on abundant Blood to stay nourished. When Blood is insufficient, the head simply does not receive enough sustenance, producing a lingering, hollow ache rather than a sharp or throbbing one. The pain often worsens when you are tired, because fatigue draws on the same limited reserves.
This pattern usually develops gradually after prolonged overwork, poor diet, or blood loss, leaving the face and lips pale and the mind foggy. The dull pain is the head's way of signaling that it is undernourished.
patterns.tongue_and_pulse: Tongue: pale, thin body with a thin white coating. Pulse: fine (Xi) and weak, like a thin thread lacking force.
patterns.why_triggers_reliefs_work: Blood is the body's nourishment; when it is scarce, any activity that draws on it-like mental strain or standing for long periods-makes the forehead pain worse. Rest and sleep allow the body to redirect its limited Blood to the head, which is why lying down brings relief. Cold and raw foods weaken the Spleen, the organ responsible for producing Blood, so keeping meals warm and regular directly supports recovery.
patterns.diet_and_lifestyle: Build Blood gently with regular meals that include dark leafy greens, red meat, liver, dates, and goji berries. Avoid skipping meals and keep raw, icy foods to a minimum, as they chill the Spleen and slow Blood production. Protect your reserves by pacing mental work and prioritizing a consistent sleep routine.

faqs.question: How does TCM know what's causing my frontal headache?
faqs.answer: TCM looks at the quality of pain, triggers, tongue appearance, and pulse. A burning, throbbing pain with bad breath points to Stomach Fire; a tight, cold-sensitive pain with chills is Wind-Cold; a heavy, foggy ache with nausea suggests Phlegm-Dampness. Your practitioner will ask detailed questions to pinpoint the pattern.

faqs.question: Can acupuncture help a frontal headache right away?
faqs.answer: Many patients feel relief during or shortly after an acupuncture session, especially for acute headaches. For chronic patterns, regular sessions reduce frequency and intensity over several weeks. Points like Yintang (between the eyebrows) and Hegu (on the hand) are often used to directly address the forehead area.

faqs.question: Do I need to change my diet?
faqs.answer: Diet plays a big role, especially for Stomach Fire and Phlegm-Dampness patterns. Cooling foods like cucumber and watermelon help clear heat, while warm, cooked meals support the Spleen. Avoiding greasy, spicy, and cold foods is often recommended. Your practitioner will give pattern-specific advice tailored to your headache type.

faqs.question: Can TCM treat headaches caused by sinus pressure?
faqs.answer: Yes. TCM sees sinus-related frontal headaches as often linked to Wind-Heat or Phlegm-Dampness obstructing the nose and forehead. Herbal formulas like Yin Qiao San and acupuncture can reduce congestion and inflammation, addressing the root rather than just drying up mucus. Many patients find their sinus symptoms improve alongside their headaches.

faqs.question: Is it safe to combine TCM with my pain medication?
faqs.answer: Generally yes, but always inform both your TCM practitioner and doctor. Some herbs like Dang Gui may interact with blood thinners. Never stop prescribed medication abruptly. TCM can reduce your reliance on painkillers over time, but this should be coordinated with your doctor.

faqs.question: How long does it take to see results?
faqs.answer: Acute headaches from external pathogens often resolve in a few days. Chronic patterns like Stomach Fire or Liver Yang Rising usually improve within 2-4 weeks of consistent herbs and acupuncture. Deficiency and dampness patterns may need 2-3 months. Many patients notice fewer and milder headaches after the first month.

faqs.question: What if my headache comes with nausea and dizziness?
faqs.answer: That often points to Phlegm-Dampness or Liver Yang Rising. Nausea suggests the Stomach and Spleen are involved, while dizziness indicates internal wind or dampness clouding the head. TCM treats the whole picture, so your formula will address both the headache and the digestive or balance issues at the same time.

research.title: Acupuncture for tension-type headache
research.description: A Cochrane systematic review of 11 randomized trials involving over 2,300 participants. It concluded that acupuncture is effective for frequent episodic and chronic tension-type headache, with a statistically significant reduction in headache days compared to routine care or sham acupuncture. Many participants had frontal pain as part of their headache pattern.
research.periodical: Linde K, Allais G, Brinkhaus B, et al. Acupuncture for tension-type headache. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2009, Issue 1. Art. No.: CD007587.

research.title: Acupuncture for chronic headache: a randomized controlled trial
research.description: This large pragmatic trial randomized 401 patients with chronic headache (mostly migraine and tension-type) to acupuncture plus usual care or usual care alone. The acupuncture group experienced significantly fewer headache days, less medication use, and fewer GP visits over 12 months, with benefits sustained at 24 months.
research.periodical: Vickers AJ, Rees RW, Zollman CE, et al. Acupuncture for chronic headache in primary care: large, pragmatic, randomised trial. BMJ 2004;328:744.

research.title: Acupuncture for migraine prophylaxis
research.description: A Cochrane review of 22 trials with over 4,400 participants. It found that acupuncture is at least as effective as prophylactic drug treatment for reducing migraine frequency, with fewer adverse effects. Although focused on migraine, the findings support acupuncture’s role for head pain that may include frontal location.
research.periodical: Linde K, Allais G, Brinkhaus B, et al. Acupuncture for migraine prophylaxis. Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2009, Issue 1. Art. No.: CD001218.
